question: Which country spans more time zones than any other nation in the world?
source_excerpt: France, including its overseas territories, has the most time zones with 12

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the answer is Russia or the USA, because they picture a single huge landmass; the tiny scattered territories of a mid-sized European country beat them both.

topicality.rationale: Geography fact about overseas territories, not news.

extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia states France, including overseas territories, has the most time zones (12, or 13 with its Antarctic claim), ahead of Russia with 11; the only caveat is that this counts overseas territories.

explanation: Twelve of them, stretching from French Polynesia in the Pacific to Réunion in the Indian Ocean. Russia and the USA manage eleven each.

question: Which country has more islands than any other on Earth, with well over two hundred thousand of them?
source_excerpt: Sweden 267,570 islands; Norway 239,057; Finland 178,947 (figures as cited in secondary sources, not verified on the Wikipedia page itself)

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Indonesia, the Philippines or Greece; the answer is a northern country most people never associate with islands at all.
extra.verification_notes: Sweden is consistently ranked first with ~222k–268k islands (Norway ~239k, second), so the answer holds; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_number_of_islands

explanation: Statistics Sweden counts around 267,000 islands, most of them tiny rocky islets along the coast and in the lakes. Norway and Finland come next, with Indonesia far behind.

question: Which country has more ancient pyramids than any other, beating even Egypt?
source_excerpt: Approximately 255 pyramids are known to have been constructed by the Nubians... more than double the number constructed in Ancient Egypt.

extra.why_interesting: Pyramids mean Egypt to almost everyone; the real record holder is its southern neighbour.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia states Sudan has about 255 Nubian pyramids, more than double Egypt's count; I found no newer source that changes this.

explanation: The Nubian kingdom of Kush built well over two hundred steep, narrow pyramids at sites like Meroë, roughly double Egypt's total.

question: Which is the only mammal capable of true, powered flight?
source_excerpt: Bats are mammals in the order Chiroptera ("hand-wing") and are the only mammals capable of true, sustained powered flight.

extra.why_interesting: Players may hesitate over flying squirrels or sugar gliders, but those only glide; the single true flyer is easy once you stop picturing gliders.
extra.verification_notes: Bats (Chiroptera) are the only mammals capable of true, sustained powered flight; gliders like flying squirrels and colugos don't qualify (https://www.pbs.org/wnet/nature/group/mammals/bat/page/2).

explanation: Flying squirrels and sugar gliders only glide downhill on skin flaps. Bats flap their way through the air for real, and there are over 1,400 species of them.

question: The shortest war in recorded history was fought in 1896, lasted under an hour, and pitted Britain against which island sultanate?
source_excerpt: considered the shortest in recorded history

extra.why_interesting: A war shorter than a lunch break sounds like a joke; the island clue lets a player reason toward an East African sultanate.
extra.verification_notes: Anglo-Zanzibar War, 27 Aug 1896, 38-45 minutes, Britain vs the Sultanate of Zanzibar, is described as the shortest recorded war.

explanation: British warships shelled the sultan's palace for about forty minutes until he surrendered. The whole war was over before the morning was.

question: Which country was the first in the world to give all adult women the right to vote, back in 1893?
source_excerpt: New Zealand became the first self-governing country in the world in which all women had the right to vote in parliamentary elections.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect a big European or American pioneer; the answer is a small colony at the far end of the world, decades ahead of Britain and the USA.
extra.verification_notes: New Zealand's 1893 Electoral Act made it the first self-governing country to give all adult women the parliamentary vote; earlier cases were territories or restricted franchises (https://nzhistory.net.nz/keyword/suffrage).

explanation: New Zealand beat Britain by a quarter of a century and the USA by 27 years. Switzerland did not get there nationally until 1971.

question: Which West African country was the last in the world to abolish slavery, doing so only in 1981?
source_excerpt: Mauritania abolished slavery in 1981, the last country to do so, and criminalised it in 2007.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume slavery was abolished everywhere in the 1800s; learning it was legal somewhere into the 1980s is a jolt.
extra.verification_notes: Mauritania is widely reported as the last country to abolish slavery (1981, criminalised 2007); no newer abolition found.

explanation: Abolition came by presidential decree in 1981, and owning slaves was not made a crime there until 2007.

question: Who was the first person ever to win two Nobel Prizes?
source_excerpt: She received a second Nobel Prize, for Chemistry, in 1911 for the discovery and study of polonium and radium.

extra.why_interesting: A well-made classic: the player feels the satisfaction of a name they know, with the payoff that she remains the only person honoured in two different sciences.
extra.verification_notes: Marie Curie won Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911, the first person to win two Nobel Prizes; no later event can change 'first'.

explanation: Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911. She is still the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

question: Which is older: the University of Oxford or the Aztec Empire?
source_excerpt: There is evidence of teaching as early as 1096, making it the oldest university in the English-speaking world

extra.why_interesting: Aztecs feel ancient and Oxford feels modern, but the university was already two centuries old when the Aztec capital was founded.
extra.verification_notes: Oxford teaching dates from 1096, while the Aztec Empire (Triple Alliance) formed in 1428 and Tenochtitlan was founded around 1325, so Oxford is older (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford).

explanation: Teaching at Oxford was under way by 1096, while the Aztecs founded Tenochtitlan in 1325. The university had been running for over two centuries before the empire existed.

question: By mass, which chemical element makes up the largest share of the human body?
source_excerpt: The average adult human body weighs around 70 kg, with 65% of this total mass being due to the element oxygen

extra.why_interesting: Players say carbon because we are 'carbon-based', or hydrogen because of water; they forget that a water molecule's mass is almost all oxygen.
extra.verification_notes: Oxygen is about 65% of human body mass, the largest share of any element; hydrogen leads only by atom count, which the question doesn't ask about (https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/106270-most-common-element-in-the-human-body-%e2%80%93-by-mass).

explanation: Around 65 percent, because the body is mostly water and the oxygen atom carries nearly all of a water molecule's weight. Carbon is a distant second.

question: Roughly how many neurons, or nerve cells, are packed into an adult human brain?
source_excerpt: 86.1 +/- 8.1 billion NeuN-positive cells ("neurons") and 84.6 +/- 9.8 billion NeuN-negative ("nonneuronal") cells.

extra.why_interesting: People know the brain is complex but have no feel for the scale; billions is enough that every person carries more neurons than there are people on Earth, several times over.
extra.verification_notes: Azevedo et al. 2009 measured about 86 billion neurons in the adult human brain, so 'About 80 billion' is the only option of the right order of magnitude (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19226510/).

explanation: About 86 billion, more than ten times the number of people on the planet, all fitting into something the size of a large grapefruit.

question: True or false: sharks were swimming in the oceans before the first trees grew on land.
source_excerpt: Sharks are older than trees

extra.why_interesting: Trees feel like the oldest living things imaginable, yet sharks were already hunting in the sea tens of millions of years before a single tree stood on land.
extra.verification_notes: Even the conservative ~420 Ma date for the oldest accepted shark scales predates the first trees (~385 Ma, Devonian); Ordovician scales (~450 Ma) are disputed but the answer holds either way (https://www.discoverwildlife.com/prehistoric-life/are-sharks-older-than-trees).

explanation: Sharks go back roughly 450 million years, while the earliest trees appeared around 385 million years ago. Sharks are also older than the rings of Saturn by some estimates.

question: In summer the Eiffel Tower stands about 15 centimetres taller than it does in winter. What causes this?
source_excerpt: specialists have estimated that the Eiffel Tower actually grows between 12 and 15 centimetres when comparing its size on cold winter days with the hottest days of summer.

extra.why_interesting: A monument changing height sounds absurd, but the explanation is everyday school physics the player already knows.

topicality.rationale: Physics fact about a landmark, evergreen.

extra.verification_notes: Thermal expansion of the iron is the accepted cause, with expert estimates of 12–15 cm seasonal growth (https://flaglerlive.com/why-the-eiffel-tower-gets-bigger-every-summer/).

explanation: Heat makes the iron expand, so on hot days the whole 300-metre structure grows by up to 15 centimetres, then shrinks back in the cold.

question: Apart from primates, which animal has fingerprints so similar to a human's that they could confuse a forensic examiner?
source_excerpt: Koala prints really do resemble human ones, but there's no evidence that investigators have actually been confused by them at a crime scene.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume only apes have fingerprints like ours; a sleepy marsupial on a different branch of the tree of life evolved them independently.
extra.verification_notes: Koalas (non-primate) have fingerprints very similar to humans per Adelaide research; researcher said they could be mixed up, though actual crime-scene confusion is unproven (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/koala-fingerprints-crime-scene/).

explanation: Koalas evolved ridged fingerprints independently, probably for gripping eucalyptus branches, and even under a microscope they are hard to tell from ours.

question: Which land animal has the longest pregnancy of any mammal, lasting nearly two years?
source_excerpt: Elephants also hold the title of the longest gestation period for any mammal, and both African species stay pregnant for 22 months.

extra.why_interesting: Nearly two years is longer than most people imagine any pregnancy could be, and the biggest land animal is the natural guess.
extra.verification_notes: Elephants have the longest mammalian gestation (~22 months); no competing land mammal or newer record found (https://www.ifaw.org/journal/animals-with-long-gestations).

explanation: Around 22 months for an African elephant, with the calf weighing about 100 kilograms at birth.

question: The green paste served as wasabi in most sushi restaurants outside Japan is actually made mostly from which other root?
source_excerpt: not authentic wasabi, but a mixture of ingredients like horseradish, mustard flour, cornstarch, and food coloring

extra.why_interesting: Players have eaten the stuff a hundred times without knowing it is a disguise; the sharp, nose-burning heat is a strong foothold toward the real ingredient.
extra.verification_notes: Restaurant 'wasabi' outside Japan is widely documented as mainly horseradish with mustard flour and green coloring; no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: Real wasabi is costly and loses its flavour within minutes of grating, so most restaurants serve horseradish with mustard and green colouring instead.

question: The croissant is a symbol of France, yet it descends from a crescent-shaped pastry invented in which other country?
source_excerpt: The kipferl, an Austrian crescent-shaped pastry, dates to at least the 13th century... the modern croissant grew out of it.

extra.why_interesting: The croissant is the symbol of a French breakfast, yet its origin lies in Vienna; a player who recalls 'Viennoiserie' can reason there.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia says the croissant descends from the Austrian kipferl, a crescent pastry dating to at least the 13th century; "invented" is loose but no other country competes.

explanation: The Viennese kipferl was brought to Paris by an Austrian baker in the 1830s, which is why French bakeries still call such pastries viennoiserie.

question: Botanists have a strict definition of a berry. Which of these fruits is NOT a berry by that definition?
source_excerpt: A strawberry is an aggregate accessory fruit. It develops from multiple ovaries in a single flower, and much of the edible flesh comes from the flower's receptacle.

extra.why_interesting: The one fruit with 'berry' in its name is the only one that botanically is not one, while the banana, which nobody would call a berry, is.
extra.verification_notes: Under the botanical definition (simple fleshy fruit from a single ovary), banana, tomato and grape are berries while strawberry is an aggregate accessory fruit, per https://sciencenotes.org/is-a-strawberry-a-berry-why-the-answer-is-surprisingly-no/

explanation: A true berry develops from a single ovary with seeds inside the flesh, which fits bananas, tomatoes and grapes. The strawberry's seeds sit on the outside, so botanically it is not a berry at all.

question: Which nut is the key ingredient in the chocolate spread Nutella?
source_excerpt: Nutella is made from sugar, modified palm oil, hazelnuts, cocoa powder, skimmed milk powder, whey powder, soy lecithin, and vanillin.

extra.why_interesting: An instant, satisfying answer for nearly everyone, with the payoff that the brand buys a huge share of the world's hazelnut crop.
extra.verification_notes: Hazelnuts are the sole nut in Nutella (about 13% of the recipe per Wikipedia), and no later development changes that.

explanation: Ferrero uses so many that it is estimated to buy around a quarter of the world's hazelnut supply, most of it grown in Turkey.

question: The Fosbury flop, a backwards technique first seen at the 1968 Olympics, revolutionised which athletics event?
source_excerpt: Fosbury won the gold medal in the high jump at the 1968 Summer Olympics using the Fosbury flop, going over the bar backward.

extra.why_interesting: The name sounds comic, but it describes the technique every elite jumper in the world now uses; players who picture athletes going over a bar backwards get it.
extra.verification_notes: Fosbury won the 1968 Olympic high jump with the backward flop, which became the standard high jump technique (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Fosbury).

explanation: Dick Fosbury won gold in Mexico City going over the bar head first and backwards, and within a few years almost every top jumper had copied him.

question: In snooker, which coloured ball is worth the most points?
source_excerpt: red 1, yellow 2, green 3, brown 4, blue 5, pink 6, black 7

extra.why_interesting: Players know the rainbow of colours on the table; working out which is the prize ball rewards anyone who has watched a frame or two.
extra.verification_notes: Black is worth 7 points, the highest-value colour, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rules_of_snooker; no newer events affect this.

explanation: The black is worth seven points, which is why a maximum break of 147 means potting fifteen reds, each followed by a black, then all the colours.

question: Which country has hosted the Summer Olympic Games more times than any other?
source_excerpt: The United States has hosted the Summer Olympics four times: 1904 St. Louis, 1932 Los Angeles, 1984 Los Angeles, 1996 Atlanta.

extra.why_interesting: Players think of London's three or Paris's three and may not realise one country has quietly outdone both.

topicality.rationale: Olympic history record, not tied to fresh news.

extra.verification_notes: The US has hosted the Summer Games 4 times (1904, 1932, 1984, 1996), ahead of France and the UK at 3 each; LA 2028 hasn't happened yet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_Games_host_cities

explanation: Four times so far, in St. Louis, Los Angeles twice and Atlanta, with Los Angeles making it five in 2028.

question: Which country has won the men's Rugby World Cup the most times?
source_excerpt: South Africa holds the record for most Rugby World Cup titles, with four, ahead of New Zealand on three.

extra.why_interesting: Most casual fans assume New Zealand's All Blacks own the record; the Springboks edged ahead in 2023.

topicality.rationale: All-time record last updated 2023; no current news hook.

extra.verification_notes: South Africa has four titles (1995, 2007, 2019, 2023), ahead of New Zealand on three, and no tournament has been played since 2023 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Rugby_World_Cup_finals).

explanation: Four titles, in 1995, 2007, 2019 and 2023. New Zealand sits on three, which surprises people who assume the All Blacks lead.

question: Which video game is the best-selling of all time, with well over three hundred million copies sold?
source_excerpt: Minecraft is the first video game to cross 300 million copies sold, comfortably holding the first-place position as the best-selling game of all time

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Tetris, Grand Theft Auto or Mario; the record holder is a blocky indie game that started with one Swedish developer.
extra.verification_notes: Mojang announced 300M+ copies in Oct 2023, far ahead of GTA V (~185M) and Tetris's usual count; no later game has overtaken it, though 'well over 300M' is slightly generous on official figures alone.

explanation: It began as a one-person project by Swedish developer Markus Persson in 2009, and Microsoft bought it for 2.5 billion dollars five years later.

question: Which film was the first in history to earn more than one billion US dollars at the worldwide box office?
source_excerpt: Titanic was the first film to pass $1 billion at the worldwide box office, and it got there on March 1, 1998.

extra.why_interesting: Players guess Star Wars or Jurassic Park; the first billion-dollar film is a romance about a sinking ship from the late 1990s.
extra.verification_notes: Titanic was the first film to pass $1B worldwide (1 March 1998); this is a historical first that later films cannot change (Guinness World Records).

explanation: James Cameron's 1997 epic crossed the billion mark in 1998 and stayed the highest-grossing film ever until his own Avatar overtook it twelve years later.

question: Which album is the best-selling of all time?
source_excerpt: Thriller... is estimated to have sold 70 million copies worldwide

extra.why_interesting: A well-made classic most players can reach, with the payoff that nothing in forty years has come close.
extra.verification_notes: Thriller is listed as the best-selling album worldwide (~70M); only the US RIAA certification ranks the Eagles' Greatest Hits higher, and the question's standard reading is worldwide.

explanation: Michael Jackson's 1982 album has sold an estimated 70 million copies worldwide, and no album released since has come close to catching it.

question: In which year was the very first text message, reading simply 'Merry Christmas', sent to a mobile phone?
source_excerpt: The first SMS, reading "Merry Christmas," was sent on 3 December 1992. Neil Papworth... sent it using a personal computer over the Vodafone GSM network

extra.why_interesting: People picture texting as a late-1990s Nokia habit, but the first message was sent years earlier, from a computer to a phone, before most people owned a mobile.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's SMS article says the first SMS, 'Merry Christmas', was sent on 3 December 1992 by Neil Papworth to an Orbitel 901 handset, which matches 1992 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SMS).

explanation: Engineer Neil Papworth typed it on a computer and sent it to a Vodafone director's phone on 3 December 1992. The phone could not even reply.

question: A modern Olympic gold medal contains only around six grams of actual gold. Which metal makes up almost all of the rest?
source_excerpt: Each medal weighs 500 grams but contains only six grams of pure gold. The remaining 494 grams are sterling silver.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a gold medal is solid gold; the answer reveals it is essentially a silver medal with a thin golden coat.

topicality.rationale: General knowledge about Olympic medal composition, not tied to any current news.

extra.verification_notes: Gold medals are about 500 g of silver plated with about 6 g of gold, and IOC rules require at least 92.5% silver (https://www.forbes.com.au/news/sport/the-2026-winter-olympics-gold-medal-is-the-most-valuable-in-history/).

explanation: The rules require at least 92.5 percent silver, with just a thin layer of gold plated on top, so the champion is really holding a gilded silver medal.

question: In 2016 scientists dated the eye lenses of a large, slow-swimming Arctic fish and estimated one individual was nearly 400 years old, making its species the longest-lived vertebrate known. Which fish is it?
source_excerpt: Greenland sharks are the longest-lived vertebrates on Earth

extra.why_interesting: Players expect tortoises or whales to hold the vertebrate longevity record; the real holder is a sluggish, half-blind shark that may have been born before Newton.

topicality.rationale: Science fact from a 2016 study, long past being news.

extra.verification_notes: The 2016 Science study (Nielsen et al.) dated Greenland shark eye lenses to ~392 years, and no newer finding supersedes the species as longest-lived vertebrate.

explanation: The sharks grow only about a centimetre a year and may not reach maturity until around 150, so the oldest one studied was likely swimming when Shakespeare was still alive.

question: The two Diomede Islands in the Bering Strait sit less than four kilometres apart, yet when it is Monday morning on one, it is still Sunday on the other. What invisible line runs between them?
source_excerpt: The International Date Line runs between them, roughly 2 km from each island; Big Diomede is nearly a day ahead of Little Diomede.

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes two islands you could row between in an hour must share a calendar, then realises the one line on Earth that flips the date happens to pass right through that narrow gap, which is also the Russia–USA border.

topicality.rationale: Timeless geography fact about the International Date Line; not tied to any news event.

extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the islands are ~3.8 km apart with the International Date Line between them and a ~21-hour time difference.

explanation: Big Diomede belongs to Russia and Little Diomede to the United States, so the line doubles as the border, and locals call them Tomorrow Island and Yesterday Isle.
